transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I came in because things have just gotten completely out of hand lately. I work down at the warehouse—been doing stocking and order filling for a good long while now, and you know, you get used to a certain rhythm. I took some college courses back in the day, so I'm no fool, but man, they just flipped everything upside down on us. 

A little while back, management decided to completely overhaul things. They changed my warehouse hours all around, and on top of that, they brought in this entirely new inventory system. Ever since they did that, I just... I feel like I’m completely falling apart. I mean, it’s not just the job, it’s my whole life right now. I’ve started missing my shifts, which isn't like me at all, I've always been a dependable worker. And it’s bleeding into the rest of my week, too. I've been skipping out on my church commitments—and I've been going there for years—but I just can't bring myself to show up or talk to anybody. 

I’m snapping at my family over the smallest little things, just biting their heads off for absolutely no reason. And the mornings... well, some mornings I just sit there on the edge of the bed, all laced up in my work boots, just staring at the floor, wondering if I can even physically bring myself to face that place anymore. I just sit there. It's just... it's all become too much to handle.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like doing?

Well, doctor, that's... that's a really good question, and honestly, it's something I've been thinking about a lot lately. You see, I used to have a whole routine, a whole set of things that just made sense to me, things I looked forward to. Like, take my garden, for instance. I've always had this little vegetable patch out back. Tomatoes, peppers, a little bit of squash—nothing fancy, but I used to love getting out there in the dirt on a Saturday morning, especially before it gets too hot, you know? Just feeling the soil, watching things grow. It gave me a real sense of accomplishment, especially after being indoors at the warehouse all week under those awful fluorescent lights.

But now? Now, I just... I look out the window at it, and I see the weeds starting to creep in, and I know I should go out there, I know I used to enjoy it, but I just can't seem to muster up the energy or the... the desire. It's like the color has been drained out of everything. Even my grandkids—they used to come over on Sundays, and we'd play cards or I'd show them how to fix little things around the house. I loved those afternoons. But lately, when my daughter calls to ask if they can come by, I find myself making excuses. I tell her I'm tired, or my back is acting up, which is true sometimes, but the real reason is I just don't feel that spark anymore. I don't feel that joy. 

It's like this heavy blanket is just draped over my whole life, and everything I used to like doing just feels like another chore on a list I can't even bear to look at. I try to read the paper, something I've done every morning for forty years, and I just end up staring at the words without taking anything in. It's just... it's all so flat now. Everything is just flat.
Do you feel anxious or on edge most of the time?

Anxious? Well, I don't know if I'd use the word anxious, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting around biting my nails or pacing holes in the living room rug, if you know what I mean. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to get anxious about things—worrying if the stove was left on, or if the kids were going to make it home before the snow started sticking to the roads. That was anxiety. She'd get all fluttery and couldn't sit still for two minutes straight. 

But me? I don't think it's that. I mean, sure, I've got a lot on my mind with all this mess at the warehouse. Who wouldn't? When you've been doing things a certain way for so long, and then some suit in an office decides to pull the rug out from under you, it makes you think. It makes you wonder what else is going to change without anyone asking your opinion on the matter. But I wouldn't say I'm sitting around feeling on edge all day long. It's more of a... a heaviness, like I was telling you before. A real heavy feeling. 

I guess sometimes when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at those boots, my stomach might do a little bit of a flip, just dreading having to walk through those doors and figure out that new computer system they put in. The screens are so bright, and the print is so small, and they expect you to just know how to use it overnight. But I wouldn't call that being on edge most of the time. It's just the thought of the place that gets to me. Once I'm home, I just feel worn down. Just completely tapped out, you know? Not jumpy, just... done.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just go to sleep and not wake up?

Well, doctor, that's... that's a heavy question. A very heavy question. And I appreciate you asking it, I really do, because I know people my age, sometimes we don't like to talk about those sorts of things. My buddy Al, he passed a few years back, and he never would have admitted to feeling down, not for a second. But me... well, I try to be honest. And honestly? No. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm miserable. I told you about how flat everything feels, how I just sit there looking at my boots in the morning. It's a terrible feeling, just this awful weight pressing down on me, making every little thing feel like moving a mountain. And sleep... well, sleep is an escape, isn't it? When I finally do manage to drift off, after tossing and turning and thinking about those new warehouse schedules and all those blinking lights on the inventory scanners... sleep is a relief. It's the only time I'm not feeling this... this crushing sense of being overwhelmed by it all. 

But wanting to not wake up? No. No, I don't want that. I just want things to go back to how they were. I want to wake up and feel like tending to my tomatoes. I want to wake up and feel like calling my daughter to see the grandkids. I want to wake up and go to work and know what I'm doing and feel like I'm contributing something, instead of feeling like I'm drowning in a puddle. I just want my life back, doctor. I don't want it to end. I just want the life I had before all this mess started. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts of wanting to be dead. Just... just thoughts of wanting things to be different. Better. Like they used to be.
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long? Well, let me think back... it's been... gosh, it's got to be about five months now. Yes, five months. Because I remember exactly when it all shifted. It was right around the time they brought in those new folks from corporate. Before that, I had my routine, you know? I knew where every single pallet was, I knew the delivery times, I knew the old paper manifests like the back of my hand. 

But then, about five months ago, they decided to completely overhaul the warehouse schedule. Just completely threw the old shifts out the window without so much as a 'by your leave' to the guys who've been working the floor for years. And that's exactly when they brought in that new inventory system I was telling you about—the one with the bright screens and the tiny print on the scanners. 

It's like somebody just flipped a switch right then and there. Ever since that new schedule and that computer system started, five months ago, I've just been... sinking. I tried to keep up at first, I really did. I even brought my reading glasses from home, the strong ones, and I tried taking notes on a little notepad I keep in my shirt pocket. I thought, 'Give it a week or two, you'll get the hang of it.' But it just kept piling on, and the expectations just kept getting more and more unreasonable. 

So, yeah, it's been a solid five months of this... this heaviness. Five months of looking at my boots in the morning and dreading having to lace them up. I keep hoping I'll wake up and they'll realize the old way was better, or that I'll suddenly feel like myself again, but... well, here we are, five months down the line, and I'm sitting in your office instead.
Do you experience physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or trembling when you think about going to work or dealing with the new inventory system?

Physical symptoms? Like my heart racing or getting all sweaty? Well, let me think about that. I know some folks get like that. My brother-in-law, Frank, he used to get the shakes so bad before he had to give a presentation at his sales job that he'd have to sit in his car for twenty minutes just doing deep breathing exercises. He'd come in and his shirt collar would be completely soaked through. But me? No, I wouldn't say I get anything like that. 

I mean, I told you about my stomach doing a little flip when I'm sitting on the edge of the bed in the morning, looking at my boots. It's just this sinking feeling, you know? Like a rock dropping right down into my gut. But it's not like my heart is pounding out of my chest or I'm breaking into a cold sweat. And I don't get the shakes. My hands are steady enough, thank the Lord, even if they are a bit arthritic these days. 

When I think about that new inventory system... well, it's more of a mental exhaustion than a physical panic. I'll be sitting in my armchair after dinner, watching the evening news, and the thought of those tiny little numbers on those bright screens will pop into my head, and I just feel... tired. Just completely drained, right down to my bones. It's like the energy just leaks right out of me. I don't start trembling or sweating or anything dramatic like that. I just feel like I'm carrying a hundred-pound sack of flour on my back, and I just want to sink into the cushions and not move. 

So, no, I don't really have those kinds of physical reactions. No racing heart, no sweating, no trembling. Just that heavy, tired feeling, and maybe that little stomach flip in the mornings. It's not a panic, doctor. It's just... it's just this awful, heavy dread.
Have you been avoiding certain tasks or situations outside of work because they remind you of the problems you're having at the warehouse?

Avoiding things outside of work because they remind me of the warehouse? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, it's not like I see a barcode at the grocery store and have to run out the door, you know? It's not the *reminder* of work that's keeping me from doing things. 

It's more just... I don't have the energy for anything anymore. Like I was saying about my tomatoes. I used to love getting out in the garden. I'd spend hours out there on a Saturday, pulling weeds, tying up the vines, checking for those little hornworms. I had a whole system for it, and it brought me a lot of joy. But now? I look out the kitchen window at those raised beds, and I just think about how much effort it would take to put my boots on and walk out there. It's not that the tomatoes remind me of the inventory scanners. Lord knows they don't. It's just that I'm so drained from dealing with all that mess at work that by the time I get home, or by the time the weekend rolls around, I've got nothing left in the tank. 

And it's the same with calling my daughter. She lives out in Ohio, and we usually talk every Sunday evening. I used to look forward to it all week, hearing about the grandkids and what they're up to. But lately, when Sunday evening comes around, I just look at the phone sitting there on the side table, and I just... I can't bring myself to pick it up. Because I know she's going to ask how I'm doing, and I don't want to lie to her, but I also don't want to burden her with all this complaining about the warehouse. She's got her own life, her own family to worry about. So I just let it go to voicemail and tell her I was busy. 

But it's not because talking to her reminds me of work. It's just that work has taken over so much of my mind, so much of my energy, that there's no room left for the things I used to enjoy. It's like that heavy feeling I told you about just spreads out and covers everything else in my life. So, no, I'm not avoiding things because they trigger some memory of the warehouse. I'm just... I'm just too exhausted and down to do much of anything else.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past five months?

Weight? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I haven't noticed any real change there. You see, I've been wearing the same size 36 waist work trousers—the heavy-duty canvas ones, you know, because the regular denim just wears right out at the knees when you're dealing with the lower pallets all day—for, gosh, it must be going on ten or twelve years now. And they still fit exactly the same. I check my belt notch every morning when I'm putting those boots on. It's the third hole from the end, same as it always is. 

Even with all this... this heaviness I was telling you about, and being so tired all the time, my stomach still expects to be fed. I still have my bowl of oatmeal every single morning, though I'll admit I haven't been putting the fresh sliced bananas on it like I used to, because I'm just too drained to bother going to the store to keep them stocked. And in the evenings, when I'm sitting in that armchair I mentioned, watching the news and trying not to think about work, sometimes I find myself just mindlessly eating a handful of salted peanuts or a couple of those oatmeal raisin cookies from the tin. It's not even because I'm really hungry, it's just... well, it's just something to do with my hands while I'm sitting there feeling so weighed down. 

So, no, the scale hasn't really budged at all. I stepped on it just last week in the bathroom—I have one of those old mechanical dial ones, not the digital kind, I don't trust the digital ones to last—and the needle was hovering right around 185. Which is exactly where it was five months ago, before all this corporate nonsense started. So no, I haven't lost a significant amount of weight. I'm carrying the exact same amount of weight on my frame, it just... it just feels a whole lot heavier to carry around these days, if you know what I mean.
Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your situation at work or your inability to cope with the changes?

Guilty? Worthless? Well... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all, doctor. I mean, why on earth should I feel guilty? I've been working hard my entire life. I did a little bit of college right out of high school, you know, but I realized pretty quick I'm a man who likes to be on his feet, getting things done, moving things around, not just sitting behind a desk listening to lectures. I’ve been a stocker and order filler for decades. I know that warehouse like the back of my own hand. If you hand me a traditional paper manifest, I can pull a pallet together faster and more accurately than any of these twenty-something kids they hire nowadays. I know exactly where everything is, from the heavy industrial solvents in aisle twelve right down to the seasonal overstock in the back corner. 

So, worthless? Absolutely not. I know the value of an honest day's work, and I've given them more than my fair share of those over the years. It’s not a failing on my part that I'm struggling so much with these changes. It’s the changes themselves! Some corporate bigwig in an air-conditioned office, probably three states away, decides we all need to use these tiny little digital scanners with screens so bright they give you a headache and buttons the size of a pinhead. And suddenly the way I've done my job perfectly well for years isn't good enough anymore. It’s just ridiculous. 

I don't feel guilty that my hands—which have a touch of arthritis, as I mentioned—don't want to punch in a twelve-digit barcode just to move a simple box of motor oil from the receiving dock to shelf B. I feel... well, I feel frustrated by it, and mostly I just feel that bone-deep exhaustion I was telling you about. It’s the sheer nonsense of it all that drains the life right out of me. But I certainly don't sit in my armchair in the evenings thinking I'm a worthless person. I know exactly what I'm worth, doctor. It's just a crying shame the company doesn't seem to value it anymore, just because I don't speak the same language as their new computer system. So, no, no guilt. No feeling worthless. Just that heavy, awful dread about having to go back in tomorrow and fight with those machines all over again.
Do you often blame yourself for not being able to adapt to the changes at work?

Blame myself? Oh, heaven's no. Why would I blame myself? Like I said, I've been doing this job, and doing it well, for a very long time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. I'm seventy-four years old. I've spent my whole life working with my hands, moving actual, physical things. I know how to read a manifest, I know how to stack a pallet so it doesn't tip when the forklift takes a corner too sharp—which, let me tell you, happens more often than management wants to admit with some of the younger drivers they hire. 

I know the physical reality of the job. So when they come in and say, "Okay, forget all that, now you have to stare at this little glowing rectangle and tap these tiny little buttons every time you move a single box," well, how is it my fault that my brain and my hands don't want to work that way? It's not a character flaw that I can't just flip a switch and become a computer expert overnight. 

I mean, I look at these young kids they bring in, they're walking around with their faces buried in their phones all day anyway, so of course tapping on a scanner comes naturally to them. But they don't know the first thing about warehouse logistics! They don't know that the heavy-duty industrial cleaner needs to be stored on the bottom rack because if a bottle leaks, it'll eat right through the cardboard of the paper goods stored underneath it. I know that. I've learned that through years of experience. 

But does the scanner know that? Does the computer system care? No. It just wants you to scan the barcode and put it in slot 42-B, regardless of what makes sense. So, no, I don't sit around blaming myself. I blame the people who decided to fix something that wasn't broken. I blame the system that treats a man with decades of practical knowledge like he's obsolete just because his thumbs aren't fast enough on a touchscreen. It's not my fault they changed the rules of the game in the fourth quarter. It's just... it's just exhausting having to play it, that's all.
Do you often feel irritable or short-tempered, even when you're not thinking about work or the warehouse?

Well, yes... yes, I suppose I do. I really do. And it bothers me, it really does, because that's not the kind of man I am. But to be completely honest with you, ever since they changed my warehouse hours—which they did right around the exact same time they put in that new digital inventory system I was telling you about—I just... I honestly feel like I'm falling apart at the seams. It's like I have absolutely no patience left in the tank for anything or anyone. 

I find myself snapping at my family over the smallest little things, things that never would have bothered me before. My wife will just ask me a simple, everyday question, like what I want for dinner or if I remembered to take the recycling bin out to the curb, and I'll just bite her head off. And the grandkids, well, they're just being kids, running around the living room and making noise like kids do, but lately the sound of it just sets my teeth on edge and I end up barking at them to quiet down. It’s terrible, it really is. I'm just so wound up and drained all at once, even on my days off. 

And it's not just the temper, doctor. It's... it's affecting everything I do. I'm actually missing shifts at the warehouse now, which is something I never, ever used to do. I've always prided myself on my attendance. But now? I'm even missing my church commitments. I've been helping set up the folding chairs and tables for the Sunday school rooms for I don't know how many years—fifteen, maybe twenty?—and lately I just haven't been showing up for it. I just can't bring myself to leave the house. 

Some mornings, it's a struggle just to get out the door. I'll get up, do my routine, have my bowl of oatmeal, and I'll sit down in the hallway to lace up my boots... and I just sit there. I'll just sit there in my work boots for twenty, thirty minutes, staring at the floorboards, just wondering if I can even face the place anymore. The thought of going in and dealing with those scanners and the new schedule... it just paralyzes me. So, yes, the short temper is definitely there, but it's really just a part of this whole... this whole falling apart that's been happening to me lately.
Do you often feel like you're a burden to others or that you're worthless as a person?

Well, like I was saying just a little bit ago about the work situation, doctor, I certainly don't feel worthless. And a burden? No, no, I really wouldn't say that either. I mean, my whole life, I've been the one carrying the load, not the other way around. I've always been the provider. Ever since my kids were little—and they're all grown up now, of course, with houses and kids of their own—I made sure there was food on the table, bills were paid on time, and everything was taken care of. 

Even now, with my wife, I'm the one who does the heavy lifting around the house. I mean, sure, I might be sitting in the hallway staring at my work boots some mornings, like I just told you, and I know I’ve been snapping at everyone, which I truly hate... but I'm not a burden to them. They know who I am. They know I've worked my fingers to the bone for this family for fifty years. 

It's just this whole mess at the warehouse that's got me tied up in knots. The schedule changes, those blasted little digital scanners... it's draining every ounce of energy I have, yes. But it hasn't made me forget who I am as a man. I'm a husband, a grandfather, a hard worker. I pay my taxes, I take care of my yard—well, mostly, though I haven't had the energy to get the mower out these past few weekends, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. But no, I don't sit around thinking I'm a burden to my family or to society. I just think I'm a man who's been pushed into a corner by a company that doesn't respect the people who built it. So, no, I don't feel like a burden, and I definitely know my worth. It's just... it's just the situation that's awful, not me.
Have you lost interest in activities you once enjoyed for more than two weeks?

Lost interest? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, if you're asking if I just don't care about the things I love anymore, that's definitely not it. 

Like I mentioned a minute ago about the yard—I haven't gotten the mower out the last couple of weekends, sure, but it's not because I don't want to or because I don't care. I still look out the front window every single morning with my coffee to check the grass. I've been using this particular blend of Kentucky Bluegrass and fescue for, oh, it has to be twenty-five years now, and I still get the seed catalogs in the mail and read them cover to cover. I still care very much about how my property looks. It's just that I'm so incredibly drained from this whole warehouse schedule mess that I just don't have the physical energy to push the mower around. But the interest? The interest is one hundred percent still there.

And it's the exact same thing with my other hobbies. I like to tinker out in the garage—refinishing old furniture, mostly. I've got this beautiful old oak rocking chair I picked up at a flea market over in the next county back in... well, it must have been early spring before all this nonsense at work started. I was making great progress on it, too. I stripped all the old, cracked varnish off, sanded it down by hand—because you can't use a power sander on those old spindles without ruining the original detail work, you know, you have to really get in there with the fine-grit paper. 

I still want to finish it. I sit in the house and I think about that chair sitting out there on my workbench under a tarp, and I want to go out and put the first coat of stain on it. I really do. I even bought the stain already, a nice dark walnut. The interest is absolutely still there. I just... I get home from dealing with those blasted digital scanners and the young managers breathing down my neck, and I just collapse into my armchair in the living room. 

So, no, my mind still wants to do all the things I've always enjoyed. I still want to go to church and set up the chairs, I still want to work on my oak rocker, I still want to have the best lawn on the block. It's just my nerves that are too shot to actually go do them right now. I haven't lost the interest, not for two weeks, not even for two days. It's just the energy, doctor. That's the difference.
Have you been avoiding social interactions or events outside of work and family?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been. Like I was telling you earlier about the church... I really have pulled back from those church duties, and that's a big social thing for me, maybe the biggest one outside of my family. And the hardest part about that, the part that really eats at me, is that people really counted on me for it. I mean, Mrs. Higgins, who runs the third-grade Sunday school class, she always expects those tables to be set up in a very specific horseshoe shape by 8:00 AM sharp. I've been the one doing that for her since her husband passed away back in, oh, it must have been 2015. But lately, I just... I don't go. I avoid the coffee hour, I avoid the men's breakfast fellowship, the whole thing. I just can't face anyone right now. I don't want them asking me how I am, or why I look so tired, or having to explain myself. 

And frankly, doctor, I know you asked about outside of work, but I have to tell you, it's all connected. It's all the same problem, because this whole avoiding things and not showing up... it's gotten to a breaking point at the warehouse, too. Just the other day, my supervisor—this young guy, probably half my age, wearing one of those quarter-zip sweaters they all wear now—he actually called me into his little glass office overlooking the loading dock. He sat me down and told me he has officially documented problems with my reliability. 

My reliability! Can you imagine? I've been working my whole life, providing for my family, and now I'm being written up for reliability by a kid who barely knows how to drive a forklift. He even went so far as to talk to me about taking a medical leave. Medical leave! I've never taken more than a day or two of sick time for a bad winter cold in my entire life. But that's just how much I've been pulling away from everything and everyone. I just can't seem to be around people or fulfill my obligations anywhere right now, whether it's at the church with people who rely on me, or down at the warehouse. It's just... I'm just hiding away from it all.
Do you often feel guilty about not being able to adapt to the changes at work?

Guilty? Well... no. No, I really don't think guilt is the right word for it at all. Frustrated, absolutely. Completely drained, like I was just saying. But guilty? No, I can't say that I do. 

I mean, let me just explain how things actually work down there on the floor. I've been doing this kind of work for a very, very long time. You don't get to be my age and still work the warehouse floor if you don't know exactly what you're doing. I know the inventory, I know the layout, I know where every single pallet is supposed to go without even having to look at a manifest. I have a system that has worked flawlessly for years. 

So when corporate decides to bring in these new digital scanners—the ones with the tiny little screens and the buttons that are just way too close together for a man wearing work gloves to press properly—and they completely overhaul the shift schedules on top of it... well, why should I feel guilty for struggling with that? If anyone should feel guilty, it's the company! They bring in these efficiency consultants, you know, these kids who have probably never lifted a fifty-pound box in their entire lives, and they just upend the whole operation to shave a few seconds off an order. 

I've tried to adapt, doctor, I really, truly have. I've stood there in the aisles squinting at that little screen until my eyes water, trying to make sense of their new routing software. But my brain just doesn't work the way those machines want it to. I'm a hands-on worker. I've always been. So, no, I don't feel guilty, because I know in my heart I'm doing my absolute best. It's their system that's unreasonable, not my work ethic. It's just... it's a deep sense of betrayal, really, that they'd treat me this way after all I've given them. But definitely not guilt.
Do you feel like your situation is getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past few months?

Better? Oh, heavens no. I wish I could sit here in this chair and tell you that things were looking up, I really do. But it's definitely not getting better. If anything, it's just getting worse, or maybe it's a constant, grinding sort of 'same' that feels worse every single day because there's absolutely no end in sight. 

You see, the real issue—the thing that's just driving me straight into the ground—is that the work changes are still going on. It wasn't just a one-and-done transition where they brought in the new scanners and the new hours and then let us settle in and get used to it. No, they're constantly tweaking things. One week they want us doing the routing one way, the next week that young efficiency consultant decides we need to shave off another three seconds, so they change the protocol all over again. 

And because of all that constant shifting, I have not had a real break from the new schedule or its fallout yet. Not a single, genuine break to just catch my breath and let my system reset. It used to be that I knew my hours—Monday through Friday, 6:00 AM to 2:00 PM, like absolute clockwork for over a decade. I built my whole life, my church duties, my yard work, around that stability. Now? I'm thrown onto these rotating shifts, sometimes a swing shift, sometimes coming in late and leaving long after dark. 

And the fallout! The mistakes the younger guys are making with those tiny scanner screens, the misplaced pallets, the delayed shipments... it all just piles up, and then we're the ones left to physically clean up the mess on the concrete floor. 

So I'm just constantly in the thick of it. I come home, I collapse in my armchair like I told you, and before I know it, I have to drag myself right back into the warehouse to face whatever new chaos they've cooked up for that shift. I haven't had a single week, not even a few days, where things were just calm and predictable. So, no, doctor, it's not getting better at all. It's just a relentless cycle, and I haven't had a moment's peace from it since this whole nightmare started.
Have you lost interest in hobbies or activities outside of work that you once enjoyed?

Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I really wouldn't. It's not that the interest is gone at all. 

Take my yard, for instance. I've always taken immense pride in my property. I have this old riding mower, bought it back in the late nineties, and I still maintain the engine myself. I still care about it. I look out the front window and I see the edging along the driveway getting a little messy, or the grass getting too high around the base of the big oak tree out front, and it bothers me. It really does. I still get my seed catalogs in the mail, and I sit there at the kitchen table with my reading glasses on, looking through them, planning out what I'd *like* to do. So the desire, the interest... it's all still right there in my head. 

It's just that... well, like I was telling you about coming home and collapsing in my armchair. I come home from whatever backwards, upside-down shift they've put me on at the warehouse, and I just sink into that chair. I want to go out to the shed, I really do. I know exactly where my pruning shears are hanging, right on the pegboard where they belong. But I just... I don't have the physical or mental gas left in the tank to actually go do it. 

It's the exact same story with my woodworking in the garage. I've got a half-finished birdhouse sitting on the workbench right now that I was making for my youngest granddaughter. I still want to finish it. I think about finishing it all the time. I haven't stopped caring about it. I just can't seem to drag myself out there to turn on the tools. 

So, no, doctor, I haven't lost interest in my hobbies at all. If anything, it just makes me incredibly frustrated that I can't get to the things I still love doing, because trying to keep my head above water at work is just taking every last ounce of what I've got.

But no, I don't sit around thinking I'm a burden to my family or to society. I just think I'm a man who's been pushed into a corner by a company that doesn't respect the people who built it. So, no, I don't feel like a burden, and I definitely know my worth. It's just... it's just the situation that's awful, not me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a loss of interest in activities they once enjoyed for more than two weeks
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in activities you once enjoyed for more than two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest in activities), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Lost interest? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, if you're asking if I just don't care about the things I love anymore, that's definitely not it. 

Like I mentioned a minute ago about the yard—I haven't gotten the mower out the last couple of weekends, sure, but it's not because I don't want to or because I don't care. I still look out the front window every single morning with my coffee to check the grass. I've been using this particular blend of Kentucky Bluegrass and fescue for, oh, it has to be twenty-five years now, and I still get the seed catalogs in the mail and read them cover to cover. I still care very much about how my property looks. It's just that I'm so incredibly drained from this whole warehouse schedule mess that I just don't have the physical energy to push the mower around. But the interest? The interest is one hundred percent still there.

And it's the exact same thing with my other hobbies. I like to tinker out in the garage—refinishing old furniture, mostly. I've got this beautiful old oak rocking chair I picked up at a flea market over in the next county back in... well, it must have been early spring before all this nonsense at work started. I was making great progress on it, too. I stripped all the old, cracked varnish off, sanded it down by hand—because you can't use a power sander on those old spindles without ruining the original detail work, you know, you have to really get in there with the fine-grit paper. 

I still want to finish it. I sit in the house and I think about that chair sitting out there on my workbench under a tarp, and I want to go out and put the first coat of stain on it. I really do. I even bought the stain already, a nice dark walnut. The interest is absolutely still there. I just... I get home from dealing with those blasted digital scanners and the young managers breathing down my neck, and I just collapse into my armchair in the living room. 

So, no, my mind still wants to do all the things I've always enjoyed. I still want to go to church and set up the chairs, I still want to work on my oak rocker, I still want to have the best lawn on the block. It's just my nerves that are too shot to actually go do them right now. I haven't lost the interest, not for two weeks, not even for two days. It's just the energy, doctor. That's the difference.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant social withdrawal
doctor.question: Have you been avoiding social interactions or events outside of work and family?

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose I have been. Like I was telling you earlier about the church... I really have pulled back from those church duties, and that's a big social thing for me, maybe the biggest one outside of my family. And the hardest part about that, the part that really eats at me, is that people really counted on me for it. I mean, Mrs. Higgins, who runs the third-grade Sunday school class, she always expects those tables to be set up in a very specific horseshoe shape by 8:00 AM sharp. I've been the one doing that for her since her husband passed away back in, oh, it must have been 2015. But lately, I just... I don't go. I avoid the coffee hour, I avoid the men's breakfast fellowship, the whole thing. I just can't face anyone right now. I don't want them asking me how I am, or why I look so tired, or having to explain myself. 

And frankly, doctor, I know you asked about outside of work, but I have to tell you, it's all connected. It's all the same problem, because this whole avoiding things and not showing up... it's gotten to a breaking point at the warehouse, too. Just the other day, my supervisor—this young guy, probably half my age, wearing one of those quarter-zip sweaters they all wear now—he actually called me into his little glass office overlooking the loading dock. He sat me down and told me he has officially documented problems with my reliability. 

My reliability! Can you imagine? I've been working my whole life, providing for my family, and now I'm being written up for reliability by a kid who barely knows how to drive a forklift. He even went so far as to talk to me about taking a medical leave. Medical leave! I've never taken more than a day or two of sick time for a bad winter cold in my entire life. But that's just how much I've been pulling away from everything and everyone. I just can't seem to be around people or fulfill my obligations anywhere right now, whether it's at the church with people who rely on me, or down at the warehouse. It's just... I'm just hiding away from it all.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of persistent feelings of worthlessness or guilt
doctor.question: Do you often feel guilty about not being able to adapt to the changes at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of guilt, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Well... no. No, I really don't think guilt is the right word for it at all. Frustrated, absolutely. Completely drained, like I was just saying. But guilty? No, I can't say that I do. 

I mean, let me just explain how things actually work down there on the floor. I've been doing this kind of work for a very, very long time. You don't get to be my age and still work the warehouse floor if you don't know exactly what you're doing. I know the inventory, I know the layout, I know where every single pallet is supposed to go without even having to look at a manifest. I have a system that has worked flawlessly for years. 

So when corporate decides to bring in these new digital scanners—the ones with the tiny little screens and the buttons that are just way too close together for a man wearing work gloves to press properly—and they completely overhaul the shift schedules on top of it... well, why should I feel guilty for struggling with that? If anyone should feel guilty, it's the company! They bring in these efficiency consultants, you know, these kids who have probably never lifted a fifty-pound box in their entire lives, and they just upend the whole operation to shave a few seconds off an order. 

I've tried to adapt, doctor, I really, truly have. I've stood there in the aisles squinting at that little screen until my eyes water, trying to make sense of their new routing software. But my brain just doesn't work the way those machines want it to. I'm a hands-on worker. I've always been. So, no, I don't feel guilty, because I know in my heart I'm doing my absolute best. It's their system that's unreasonable, not my work ethic. It's just... it's a deep sense of betrayal, really, that they'd treat me this way after all I've given them. But definitely not guilt.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is improving or worsening over time
doctor.question: Do you feel like your situation is getting better, worse, or staying about the same over the past few months?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: The work changes are still going on, and I have not had a real break from the new schedule or its fallout yet.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the progression of the patient's situation (whether it is resolving or persisting), which aligns with the ongoing nature of the stressor and the lack of a break or resolution described in Additional Requirement 2.

patient.answer:
Better? Oh, heavens no. I wish I could sit here in this chair and tell you that things were looking up, I really do. But it's definitely not getting better. If anything, it's just getting worse, or maybe it's a constant, grinding sort of 'same' that feels worse every single day because there's absolutely no end in sight. 

You see, the real issue—the thing that's just driving me straight into the ground—is that the work changes are still going on. It wasn't just a one-and-done transition where they brought in the new scanners and the new hours and then let us settle in and get used to it. No, they're constantly tweaking things. One week they want us doing the routing one way, the next week that young efficiency consultant decides we need to shave off another three seconds, so they change the protocol all over again. 

And because of all that constant shifting, I have not had a real break from the new schedule or its fallout yet. Not a single, genuine break to just catch my breath and let my system reset. It used to be that I knew my hours—Monday through Friday, 6:00 AM to 2:00 PM, like absolute clockwork for over a decade. I built my whole life, my church duties, my yard work, around that stability. Now? I'm thrown onto these rotating shifts, sometimes a swing shift, sometimes coming in late and leaving long after dark. 

And the fallout! The mistakes the younger guys are making with those tiny scanner screens, the misplaced pallets, the delayed shipments... it all just piles up, and then we're the ones left to physically clean up the mess on the concrete floor. 

So I'm just constantly in the thick of it. I come home, I collapse in my armchair like I told you, and before I know it, I have to drag myself right back into the warehouse to face whatever new chaos they've cooked up for that shift. I haven't had a single week, not even a few days, where things were just calm and predictable. So, no, doctor, it's not getting better at all. It's just a relentless cycle, and I haven't had a moment's peace from it since this whole nightmare started.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in hobbies or activities (anhedonia), which is typically a symptom of depression. My symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder does not include a specific item for loss of interest in hobbies.

patient.answer:
Lost interest? No, I wouldn't say that. I really wouldn't. It's not that the interest is gone at all. 

Take my yard, for instance. I've always taken immense pride in my property. I have this old riding mower, bought it back in the late nineties, and I still maintain the engine myself. I still care about it. I look out the front window and I see the edging along the driveway getting a little messy, or the grass getting too high around the base of the big oak tree out front, and it bothers me. It really does. I still get my seed catalogs in the mail, and I sit there at the kitchen table with my reading glasses on, looking through them, planning out what I'd *like* to do. So the desire, the interest... it's all still right there in my head. 

It's just that... well, like I was telling you about coming home and collapsing in my armchair. I come home from whatever backwards, upside-down shift they've put me on at the warehouse, and I just sink into that chair. I want to go out to the shed, I really do. I know exactly where my pruning shears are hanging, right on the pegboard where they belong. But I just... I don't have the physical or mental gas left in the tank to actually go do it. 

It's the exact same story with my woodworking in the garage. I've got a half-finished birdhouse sitting on the workbench right now that I was making for my youngest granddaughter. I still want to finish it. I think about finishing it all the time. I haven't stopped caring about it. I just can't seem to drag myself out there to turn on the tools. 

So, no, doctor, I haven't lost interest in my hobbies at all. If anything, it just makes me incredibly frustrated that I can't get to the things I still love doing, because trying to keep my head above water at work is just taking every last ounce of what I've got.

patient.answer:
Improving, staying the same, getting worse... you know, I... I honestly couldn't tell you. I really couldn't give you a clear answer on that, doctor. Because to know if something is changing, you have to be able to measure it, right? You have to have some sort of baseline. But these past few weeks... they just blur together into one long, exhausting stretch. 

When they have you on these rotating schedules—like last week, for instance, they had me coming in at 4:00 PM and leaving at midnight, and then this week it's 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM—your body doesn't even know what day it is anymore. I'll wake up in that armchair of mine, the one I was telling you about, and for a good five minutes, I genuinely don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Thursday evening. I have to look out the front window to see if the sun is coming up or going down just to orient myself. 

So, my energy levels? My mood? It's all just... a fog. A thick, heavy, gray fog. I don't know if the fog is thicker today than it was three weeks ago. I haven't really noticed a trend one way or the other because I'm just so focused on putting one foot in front of the other. Some days I wake up and I think, 'Okay, maybe I can handle this new routing software today,' and I feel a tiny bit of a spark. But then I get to the warehouse, and someone's left the pallet jack uncharged, or the efficiency kids have moved the staging area again, and whatever little bit of energy I thought I had is just snuffed right out before my shift even really starts. 

So is that worse? Is it exactly the same as it was a month ago? I really don't know. I don't know how to quantify it for you. I haven't had the presence of mind to sit back and evaluate my mood, because I'm just trying to survive the week. I just know that I'm tired, deep down in my bones, and I couldn't tell you if it's a different kind of tired than it was at the start of the month.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had any recent changes in appetite
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite over the past few months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Appetite? Well, let me think on that for a second... No, I wouldn't say my appetite has changed. Not the actual desire for food, anyway. 

I mean, the *schedule* of when I eat is completely turned upside down, just like everything else I've been telling you about. It used to be I had my routine, you know? I’d wake up, have a bowl of oatmeal at 5:00 AM, head to the warehouse, and then at exactly 10:30 AM I’d be in the breakroom with my lunch cooler. I'd sit in the exact same chair, have a turkey sandwich, maybe an apple, and a thermos of black coffee. Every single day, regular as a metronome. 

But now, with these crazy swing shifts and late nights, half the time I’m eating what you’d call 'dinner' at three in the afternoon, or I'm sitting on a stack of pallets at midnight trying to choke down a cold sandwich while those efficiency kids are running around shouting about the new routing protocols. It completely throws off your whole system, eating at those odd hours under those buzzing fluorescent lights. 

But as far as the appetite itself goes? No, I'm still eating about the same amount. I have to, really. I'm burning so much physical and mental energy just trying to keep up, dragging my feet across that concrete floor, dealing with all the misplaced shipments... if I didn't eat, I'd probably just keel over right there in the loading bay. Food is just fuel for the engine, and the engine is working absolute overtime right now. So I still get hungry, I still finish whatever I pack for my shift, and I haven't noticed myself eating any more or any less than I did before all this nonsense started.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had any recent significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost any weight recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight loss, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Weight? No, no, I haven't lost any weight. Not a pound, as far as I can tell. 

I don't weigh myself every single day, mind you, but I've got this old dial scale in the master bathroom. Bought it at Sears, oh, it must have been twenty years ago now. One of the sturdy ones, not like the cheap digital plastic things they sell today. Every now and then I'll step on it after a shower, and that needle goes right up to the exact same number it has for the last decade. 

And you know, you can always tell by your clothes, right? I wear these heavy-duty work jeans to the warehouse. The kind with the double-layered denim on the knees, because you're always having to crouch down on that freezing concrete to check the lower storage racks or pick up something somebody dropped. I've got five pairs of them in rotation, and they all fit exactly the same around the waist as they did before all this schedule nonsense started. I use this thick leather belt—had it forever—and I'm still buckling it on the exact same notch. The third hole from the end. You can see the wear mark right on the leather where the brass buckle sits. It hasn't moved an inch. 

You'd think, honestly, with how much they have me running around... I mean, that warehouse is massive, easily the size of three football fields. And with the new routing software sending everything to the wrong loading bays, I'm walking twice as much as I used to, just trying to track down missing inventory because the computer says it's in aisle four when it's actually sitting on a pallet in aisle twelve. You'd think a man my age would drop a few pounds from all that extra mileage. 

But like I was just saying about my meals, I'm eating enough to keep the engine running. The fuel goes in, the energy gets burned up out there on the floor, and my weight just stays exactly the same. So, no, no weight loss to report.
